name: In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation
impact_assessment: joint impact assessment SWD(2012) 273 (executive summary SWD(2012) 274)
evidence_rating: thin: one monitoring survey of manufacturers, single-laboratory inventories of in-house tests and interview studies; no causal study
summary: The Regulation has applied since May 2022, with long transition periods because most tests now need a notified body. In the Commission's monitoring survey, 61% of responding manufacturers of in vitro diagnostics had withdrawn some tests since 2022. Hospital laboratories rely heavily on tests they make themselves, which the Regulation restricts: 47% of the tests used at one Belgian university hospital. The Commission's 2025 evaluation of both device regulations found high and often disproportionate costs; the December 2025 proposal would simplify both.

indicators.objective: No monitoring indicators set in the proposal; assessed through the Commission's reports listed below

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), Targeted evaluation of Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices, SWD(2025) 1051
literature.title: Targeted evaluation of Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices
literature.outcomes: safety; compliance costs; device availability; innovation
literature.headline: Benefits for patients materialising through stronger safety, performance and transparency, but at high and often disproportionate cost; implementation delays, longer and costlier market access, limited notified-body capacity; decrease in availability of some, particularly innovative and niche, devices
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's own evaluation found the stricter rules make devices safer and more transparent, but are costly and slow enough that some devices, especially new and niche ones, have left or not reached the EU market.
literature.quality: Commission self-assessment; data on costs limited

literature.citation: European Commission (2025), Cost-savings accompanying the proposal amending Regulations (EU) 2017/745 and 2017/746, SWD(2025) 1050
literature.title: Cost-savings accompanying the proposal amending Regulations (EU) 2017/745 and 2017/746
literature.headline: Simplification measures in the December 2025 proposal estimated to save around EUR 3.3 billion a year (EUR 0.9 billion adjustment and EUR 2.4 billion administrative costs)
literature.summary_plain: For its proposed simplification, the Commission estimates savings for industry of about EUR 3.3 billion a year.

literature.citation: Austrian National Public Health Institute (GÖG); Areté; Civic Consulting (2026), Study supporting the monitoring of availability of medical devices on the EU market - 3rd economic operator survey (IVD results, data status 31 October 2025), Report for European Commission DG SANTE / HaDEA
literature.authors: Austrian National Public Health Institute (GÖG); Areté; Civic Consulting
literature.title: Study supporting the monitoring of availability of medical devices on the EU market - 3rd economic operator survey (IVD results, data status 31 October 2025)
literature.venue: Report for European Commission DG SANTE / HaDEA
literature.method: online survey of IVD manufacturers (n=49 for discontinuation items)
literature.outcomes: discontinuation of IVDs from the EU market; planned discontinuations; orphan/niche tests
literature.headline: 61% of responding IVD manufacturers (30/49) had stopped producing, marketing or supplying some IVDs on the EU market since 2022, and 45% (22/49) planned further discontinuations. No respondent said orphan or niche IVDs had been affected so far, but 2 of 22 expected them to be.
literature.summary_plain: Most diagnostic-test makers in the Commission's monitoring survey have already dropped some tests from the EU market, and almost half plan to drop more.

literature.citation: Vermeersch, P.; Van Aelst, T.; Dequeker, E.M.C. (2020), The new IVD Regulation 2017/746: a case study at a large university hospital laboratory in Belgium demonstrates the need for clarification on the degrees of freedom laboratories have to use lab-developed tests to improve patient care, Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine 59(1):101-106
literature.authors: Vermeersch, P.; Van Aelst, T.; Dequeker, E.M.C.
literature.title: The new IVD Regulation 2017/746: a case study at a large university hospital laboratory in Belgium demonstrates the need for clarification on the degrees of freedom laboratories have to use lab-developed tests to improve patient care
literature.method: classification of all 922 tests in one university hospital lab by regulatory status
literature.outcomes: share of CE-IVD vs lab-developed tests (exposure to Art 5(5))
literature.headline: 97.6% of over 11.5 million results/year came from CE-IVD methods, but only 41.8% of the 922 distinct tests were CE-IVD and 47.1% were lab-developed tests. For 71.5% of the 537 LDTs outside the old directive's scope there was no commercial alternative.
literature.summary_plain: Before the IVDR applied, nearly half the distinct tests in a big hospital lab were home-made, and most had no commercial substitute, so the new in-house-test rules would hit many tests.

literature.citation: Gaja-Lachman, S.; De Visser-Timmermans, M.; Langerak, D.; Jansma, A.; Yusuf, E. (2026), From compliance to complexity: the impact of in vitro diagnostic regulation for clinical microbiology laboratories, Clinical Microbiology and Infection 32(7):1179-1182
literature.authors: Gaja-Lachman, S.; De Visser-Timmermans, M.; Langerak, D.; Jansma, A.; Yusuf, E.
literature.title: From compliance to complexity: the impact of in vitro diagnostic regulation for clinical microbiology laboratories
literature.method: test-inventory analysis of one academic clinical microbiology laboratory
literature.outcomes: share of tests and results relying on CE-IVD vs LDTs
literature.headline: In bacteriology, CE-IVD tests were 55% (57/104) of available tests but 82.8% of results. 38% of mycology tests were LDTs, and only 29% (7/24) of parasitology tests had a CE-IVD label.
literature.summary_plain: In a Dutch hospital microbiology lab, many tests, especially for fungi and parasites, depend on home-made assays that the IVDR's in-house rules make harder to keep.
literature.quality: descriptive; single site; measures exposure, not outcomes

literature.citation: Hermans, A.M.M.; Maliepaard, M.; Boon, W.P.C.; Pasmooij, A.M.G. (2022), Impact of the new European Union In Vitro Diagnostics Regulation on the practice of hospital diagnostic laboratories, Expert Review of Molecular Diagnostics 22(5):583-590
literature.authors: Hermans, A.M.M.; Maliepaard, M.; Boon, W.P.C.; Pasmooij, A.M.G.
literature.title: Impact of the new European Union In Vitro Diagnostics Regulation on the practice of hospital diagnostic laboratories
literature.method: semi-structured interviews in 15 Dutch hospital laboratories (7 academic, 8 general)
literature.outcomes: use of in-house vs commercial companion diagnostics; expected IVDR effects
literature.headline: Labs welcomed higher CDx quality but worried about higher costs, administrative work and lower quality. The IVDR 'might also hinder using optimized in-house and tweaked CDx' and could reduce innovation in companion diagnostics.
literature.summary_plain: Hospital labs expect the IVDR to make their home-adapted cancer-drug tests harder and costlier to use.
literature.quality: qualitative; anticipatory (largely ex-ante perceptions); authors include Dutch medicines regulator staff

literature.citation: MedTech Europe (2025), MedTech Europe IVDR & MDR Survey Results 2024 - Report Highlights (IVD results), MedTech Europe report
literature.title: MedTech Europe IVDR & MDR Survey Results 2024 - Report Highlights (IVD results)
literature.method: online survey of 73 IVD manufacturers, Apr-May 2024
literature.outcomes: certification time; first-launch geography; orphan devices
literature.headline: IVDR QMS or technical documentation certification took about 18 months on average. Choosing the EU as first-launch market fell from 85% to 45% for large IVD firms and from 92% to 80% for SMEs, and 26.6% of IVD makers of orphan devices said they would transition less than 5% of them.
literature.summary_plain: Diagnostic-test makers report that IVDR certification takes about 18 months and that far fewer now launch new tests in Europe first.

literature.citation: McDermott, O.; Folan, M.; Stafylas, P.C. (2026), An impact assessment of the European medical device regulations implementation - the current status quo, Expert Review of Medical Devices 23(9):1137-1148
literature.authors: McDermott, O.; Folan, M.; Stafylas, P.C.
literature.title: An impact assessment of the European medical device regulations implementation - the current status quo
literature.method: quantitative survey of MD and IVD enterprises
literature.outcomes: launch location; portfolio rationalisation; costs (MDR and IVDR pooled)
literature.headline: Finds the MDR/IVDR 'has harmed innovation', with firms launching elsewhere first, removing devices and facing higher NB, documentation and staffing costs. The abstract pools MDR and IVDR.
literature.summary_plain: Survey of device and diagnostics firms reports more launches outside Europe and dropped products under the new rules.
literature.quality: descriptive; self-report; MDR and IVDR not separated in abstract
